variants.name: Routine life, low institutional trust
variants.text: Simulated respondents find daily life routine yet pretty happy, and keep social contact modest, mostly a few evenings a month or year. They hold middling-to-low trust in institutions and in other people, and tend to be wary of politics without being disengaged. Their views on family and work are mixed, and they are cautious rather than enthusiastic about technology and AI.

variants.name: Stable finances, skeptical of democracy
variants.text: These respondents describe their finances as stable, with income placed around average or below and little recent change. They are dissatisfied with how democracy works while still paying close attention to political news and checking claims online. Their outlook on the economy and tax burden runs negative, and their attitudes toward technology and robots vary from concerned to neutral.

variants.name: Cautious, ambivalent, middling outlook
variants.text: Answers cluster around the midpoint on many scales: moderate trust, neither clearly positive nor negative views of the economy, and mixed agreement on statements about work and family. Respondents report being pretty happy but not excited by life, and their social time is infrequent. Their attitudes toward AI and automation are split, with reservations that shift case by case rather than a single firm stance.

variants.name: Distrustful and disengaged from politics
variants.text: Simulated respondents combine deep suspicion of other people and institutions with low political engagement and dissatisfaction with how democracy works. Their wariness of others tends to go together with frequent self-checking of political information and a sense that the system is not serving them. They express low trust across the board while still being only moderately interested in politics overall.

variants.name: Financially strained but socially steady
variants.text: Simulated respondents report a worsening household financial situation and a pessimistic view of the economy, yet their everyday life feels routine rather than exciting. Money stress and a bleak outlook go together with a sense of ordinary contentment and modest, predictable social lives. Their general happiness is middling, and they hold fairly conventional views on taxes and family roles.

variants.name: Uneasy about technology and automation
variants.text: Simulated respondents are strongly divided on technology: they lean toward worry about robots and AI and are uncomfortable with machines performing human tasks, while also endorsing technology in general. This discomfort tends to sit alongside skepticism toward scientific spending and a belief that other people cannot be trusted. Their views on automation are the most extreme part of the profile, with mixed feelings elsewhere.

variants.name: Financially strained, quietly disengaged
variants.text: Respondents feel their family finances have worsened and sit below average, seeing themselves as middle class but pessimistic about the national economy. They report low interest in politics and dissatisfaction with how democracy works, paired with a muted, not-too-happy outlook on life that they describe as dull. Their social lives are narrow, rarely extending beyond the neighborhood, while they keep occasional family contact. Overall they lean toward withdrawal rather than active engagement.

variants.name: Trusting yet cynical about institutions
variants.text: These people hold a fairly generous general trust in others while giving middling, unenthusiastic ratings to public institutions. They rarely verify political information online, suggesting they take sources at face value rather than investigating them. Their views on technology are mixed: they are uneasy about automation and artificial intelligence in daily life, yet they are comfortable with the tax burden and feel that science receives too little support. The pattern is cautious optimism about people combined with detachment from formal civic systems.

variants.name: Traditional family-focused skeptics
variants.text: Their answers cluster around a view that work pressures harm family life, and they prioritise home obligations over outside social networks. They are wary of new technology and strongly worried about robots and AI, while not wanting them to take over human activities. They feel neither tax nor policy burdens are unfair, yet they judge the economy poorly and rarely find life exciting. The defining feature is a home-centred, somewhat anxious orientation toward change.
